items.title: 2.2.1 Intersection of a Linear Function and Coordinate Axes

blocks.text: As we know that linear function is a function in which the highest power of the variable is one. While the coordinate axes refers to \(x\)-axis and \(y\)-axis in the Cartesian coordinate system.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
A linear function has the form \(y = mx + c\) (for example \(y = 2x + 6\)); its graph is a straight line. To draw a straight line, two points are enough; a third point is a useful check.
Every point on the \(x\)-axis has \(y = 0\), and every point on the \(y\)-axis has \(x = 0\). So:
the line meets the \(x\)-axis where \(y = 0\) (the \(x\)-intercept), and
the line meets the \(y\)-axis where \(x = 0\) (the \(y\)-intercept).

blocks.title: Example 7
blocks.problem: Find the points of intersection of a linear function \(y = 2x + 6\) and coordinate axes.
steps:
Given: the linear function \(y = 2x + 6\).
To find: the points where its graph meets the \(x\)-axis and the \(y\)-axis.
Method: make a table of values, plot the points and draw the line (as the book does), then read where the line crosses each axis. Check the readings with \(y = 0\) and \(x = 0\).

Step 1: Make a table of values
Choose \(x = -1, 0, 1\) and find \(y\):
\[x = -1:\ y = 2(-1) + 6 = 4\]
\[x = 0:\ y = 2(0) + 6 = 6\]
\[x = 1:\ y = 2(1) + 6 = 8\]
Why: each \(x\) gives one point \((x, y)\) on the line. Small values of \(x\) keep the arithmetic easy.

Step 2: Plot the points and draw the line
Plot \((-1, 4)\), \((0, 6)\) and \((1, 8)\) and join them with a ruler, extending the line in both directions (see the table and graph below).
Why: the graph of a linear function is a straight line; all three points lie on it, which confirms the table has no slip.

Step 3: Read the points on the axes
The line crosses the \(x\)-axis at \((-3, 0)\) and the \(y\)-axis at \((0, 6)\).
Why: a point on the \(x\)-axis has \(y = 0\); a point on the \(y\)-axis has \(x = 0\).

Check:
Put \(y = 0\):
\[0 = 2x + 6\]
\[2x = -6 \Rightarrow x = -3\]
Put \(x = 0\):
\[y = 2(0) + 6 = 6\]
Both agree with the graph: \((-3, 0)\) and \((0, 6)\).
blocks.answer: The line \(y = 2x + 6\) meets the \(x\)-axis at \((-3, 0)\) and the \(y\)-axis at \((0, 6)\).

blocks.caption: Table (as printed in the book): values of y = 2x + 6

blocks.alt: Graph of the line y = 2x + 6 on axes marked from minus 4 to 4 (x) and minus 4 to 8 (y). The plotted points are (minus 1, 4), (0, 6) and (1, 8). The line cuts the x-axis at (minus 3, 0) and the y-axis at (0, 6).
blocks.caption: Figure: graph of y = 2x + 6 meeting the axes at (−3, 0) and (0, 6) (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.text: Hence, from the above graph, the points \((-3, 0)\) and \((0, 6)\) are the points of intersections of \(y = 2x + 6\) and coordinate axes.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. A linear function \(y = mx + c\) has a straight-line graph.
2. \(x\)-intercept: put \(y = 0\); \(y\)-intercept: put \(x = 0\).
3. For \(y = mx + c\) the \(y\)-intercept is always \((0, c)\).
4. Two points draw the line; a third point checks it.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Swapping the coordinates: the \(x\)-intercept of \(y = 2x + 6\) is \((-3, 0)\), not \((0, -3)\).
2. Sign slip when solving \(0 = 2x + 6\): \(x = -3\), not \(3\).
3. Stopping the line at the plotted points: extend it until it crosses both axes.
